results.question: A $20/mo product wants to add annual billing. Is a 12-months-for-the-price-of-10 discount too generous, or not generous enough to change behaviour?

columns.text:
PICK: Not generous enough

WHY: Two months free (~17% off) is the industry norm, not a giveaway, because annual prepay cuts churn and brings cash forward, which usually more than pays for the discount. If anything it sits at the low end of what moves fence-sitters, so you'd lean toward strengthening the offer (e.g., framing it as "2 months free" or testing ~20%) rather than shrinking it.
columns.why: Two months free (~17% off) is the industry norm, not a giveaway, because annual prepay cuts churn and brings cash forward, which usually more than pays for the discount. If anything it sits at the low end of what moves fence-sitters, so you'd lean toward strengthening the offer (e.g., framing it as "2 months free" or testing ~20%) rather than shrinking it.

columns.text:
PICK: Too generous
WHY: You’re giving up 16.7% of annual revenue even for customers who would prepay for less. Start with one month free, then offer two only if the additional annual conversions and retention gains justify the extra discount.
columns.why: You’re giving up 16.7% of annual revenue even for customers who would prepay for less. Start with one month free, then offer two only if the additional annual conversions and retention gains justify the extra discount.

columns.text:
PICK: Not generous enough
WHY: A 16.7% discount only saves the user $40 over a full year, which is rarely enough absolute dollar value to overcome the friction of paying $200 upfront instead of $20. To meaningfully shift behavior at low price points, annual plans usually require at least a 20% to 25% discount (e.g., $180/year or 3 months free) to create a compelling psychological anchor.
columns.why: A 16.7% discount only saves the user $40 over a full year, which is rarely enough absolute dollar value to overcome the friction of paying $200 upfront instead of $20. To meaningfully shift behavior at low price points, annual plans usually require at least a 20% to 25% discount (e.g., $180/year or 3 months free) to create a compelling psychological anchor.

columns.text:
PICK: Not generous enough
WHY: A 16.67% discount may not be sufficient to incentivize customers to switch to annual billing, as it is relatively standard in the industry. More significant discounts, such as 20-25%, are often more effective at changing behavior.
columns.why: A 16.67% discount may not be sufficient to incentivize customers to switch to annual billing, as it is relatively standard in the industry. More significant discounts, such as 20-25%, are often more effective at changing behavior.

columns.text:
PICK: Too generous
WHY: A 20% discount is substantial and may unnecessarily reduce revenue when a smaller incentive could still drive annual conversions. Many businesses offer only 10-15% for annual billing, which is often sufficient to change behavior.
columns.why: A 20% discount is substantial and may unnecessarily reduce revenue when a smaller incentive could still drive annual conversions. Many businesses offer only 10-15% for annual billing, which is often sufficient to change behavior.

results.verdict: Claude Opus 5.5 and Gemini 4 both provided similar insights, suggesting that the discount is not generous enough, which aligns with industry standards for encouraging annual billing. GPT-6 Astra, however, argued that the discount is too generous, which contrasts with the consensus and reflects a different perspective on revenue loss versus customer behavior.

results.question: An agency owner at $30k/mo revenue is the bottleneck on delivery. Hire a full-time employee, or scale with contractors?

columns.text:
PICK: Full-time hire
WHY: If the owner is the delivery bottleneck, contractors usually still need the owner to brief, manage, and QA their work, so the bottleneck stays in place. A full-time hire, such as a delivery lead or senior generalist, can absorb process knowledge, own client outcomes, and free the owner for sales, and $30k/mo can typically support that salary.

A full-time hire, such as a delivery lead or senior generalist, can absorb process knowledge, own client outcomes, and free the owner for sales, and $30k/mo can typically support that salary.

columns.text:
PICK: Contractors
WHY: At $30k/mo, contractors let you add delivery capacity without committing to full-time payroll before margins and workload justify it. Give an experienced contractor ownership of a clearly scoped delivery function—not just tasks—or you’ll remain the bottleneck.
columns.why: At $30k/mo, contractors let you add delivery capacity without committing to full-time payroll before margins and workload justify it. Give an experienced contractor ownership of a clearly scoped delivery function—not just tasks—or you’ll remain the bottleneck.

columns.text:

columns.why: A full-time hire provides consistent availability and deeper integration into your processes, reducing the bottleneck more effectively than managing multiple contractors. This ensures reliable delivery as you scale.

results.verdict: Claude Opus 5.5 served the user best by addressing the core issue of the owner being the bottleneck and recommending a full-time hire that can alleviate that problem effectively. results.question: For a new Next.js App Router product with heavy interactivity, should most components default to Server Components, or is a mostly-client architecture more honest about the app's needs?

columns.text:
PICK: Server Components by default
WHY: Even highly interactive apps have large static or data-fetching shells (layouts, data loading, auth gates). Keeping those on the server while pushing "use client" down to interactive leaves cuts bundle size and keeps data access simple without limiting interactivity.
columns.why: Even highly interactive apps have large static or data-fetching shells (layouts, data loading, auth gates). Keeping those on the server while pushing "use client" down to interactive leaves cuts bundle size and keeps data access simple without limiting interactivity.

columns.text:
PICK: Server Components by default
WHY: Heavy interactivity warrants substantial Client Component subtrees, not making every component client-side. Keep layouts and server-side data access in Server Components, and use client boundaries wherever state, effects, or browser APIs are needed.
columns.why: Heavy interactivity warrants substantial Client Component subtrees, not making every component client-side. Keep layouts and server-side data access in Server Components, and use client boundaries wherever state, effects, or browser APIs are needed.

columns.text:
PICK: Server Components by default
WHY: Even in heavily interactive applications, defaulting to Server Components for layouts, routing, and initial data fetching minimizes client bundle sizes and simplifies data access. You can then deliberately push `"use client"` boundaries down to the specific interactive leaf nodes or feature subtrees, getting the best of both worlds without fighting the App Router's design.
columns.why: Even in heavily interactive applications, defaulting to Server Components for layouts, routing, and initial data fetching minimizes client bundle sizes and simplifies data access. You can then deliberately push `"use client"` boundaries down to the specific interactive leaf nodes or feature subtrees, getting the best of both worlds without fighting the App Router's design.

columns.text:
PICK: Mostly client
WHY: A heavily interactive application likely requires a significant amount of client-side JavaScript to handle user interactions, making a mostly-client architecture more suitable. Defaulting to Server Components might lead to unnecessary complexity with client-side interactivity.
columns.why: A heavily interactive application likely requires a significant amount of client-side JavaScript to handle user interactions, making a mostly-client architecture more suitable. Defaulting to Server Components might lead to unnecessary complexity with client-side interactivity.

columns.text:
PICK: Server Components by default
WHY: Server Components reduce client-side JavaScript and improve initial load performance, while still allowing strategic use of Client Components for interactivity where needed.
columns.why: Server Components reduce client-side JavaScript and improve initial load performance, while still allowing strategic use of Client Components for interactivity where needed.

results.question: Should an AI code reviewer be allowed to block a pull request from merging, or should it only ever leave advisory comments?

columns.text:
PICK: Advisory only
WHY: AI reviewers still produce enough false positives and non-deterministic judgments that hard-blocking would erode trust and train developers to game or bypass the tool. Merge gates should rest on deterministic checks (tests, linters, security scanners) and accountable human approvers, with AI comments informing those humans rather than overruling them.
columns.why: AI reviewers still produce enough false positives and non-deterministic judgments that hard-blocking would erode trust and train developers to game or bypass the tool. Merge gates should rest on deterministic checks (tests, linters, security scanners) and accountable human approvers, with AI comments informing those humans rather than overruling them.

columns.text:
PICK: Allowed to block
WHY: Blocking can prevent serious security or correctness defects before they reach production. That authority should be limited by human-defined criteria, supported by verifiable evidence, and subject to human override.
columns.why: Blocking can prevent serious security or correctness defects before they reach production. That authority should be limited by human-defined criteria, supported by verifiable evidence, and subject to human override.

columns.text:
PICK: Advisory only
WHY: AI models frequently hallucinate and lack full architectural context, meaning blocking capabilities would introduce unacceptable friction and bottleneck deployments due to false positives. Deterministic checks like compilers, linters, and test suites should handle automated blocking, while final merge authority must remain with accountable human engineers.
columns.why: AI models frequently hallucinate and lack full architectural context, meaning blocking capabilities would introduce unacceptable friction and bottleneck deployments due to false positives. Deterministic checks like compilers, linters, and test suites should handle automated blocking, while final merge authority must remain with accountable human engineers.

columns.text:
PICK: Advisory only
WHY: An AI code reviewer should not have the final say in blocking a pull request as it may not fully understand the context or nuances of the code change, and human judgment is still essential for critical decisions. Allowing AI to block merges could lead to unnecessary delays or incorrect rejections.
columns.why: An AI code reviewer should not have the final say in blocking a pull request as it may not fully understand the context or nuances of the code change, and human judgment is still essential for critical decisions. Allowing AI to block merges could lead to unnecessary delays or incorrect rejections.

columns.text:
PICK: Advisory only
WHY: An AI code reviewer should provide recommendations and highlight potential issues, but final approval and responsibility should remain with human developers to ensure context, intent, and nuanced judgment are properly considered.
columns.why: An AI code reviewer should provide recommendations and highlight potential issues, but final approval and responsibility should remain with human developers to ensure context, intent, and nuanced judgment are properly considered.

results.verdict: Claude Opus 5.5 and Gemini 4 both provided a strong argument for AI reviewers being advisory only, emphasizing the risks of false positives and the importance of human oversight, making their answers more aligned and effective for the user's question. In contrast, GPT-6 Astra advocated for allowing AI to block merges, which introduces a different perspective but lacks the consensus on the risks highlighted by the other two models.

results.question: You need a model to answer questions over a 500-page internal handbook that changes monthly. Build RAG, or just stuff it into a long context window?

columns.text:
PICK: Build RAG
WHY: A 500-page handbook runs roughly 250–400k tokens, so sending all of it with every query is slow and expensive, and accuracy tends to drop when the answer is buried in the middle. Re-indexing once a month is cheap, and retrieval lets you cite the exact section behind each answer.
columns.why: A 500-page handbook runs roughly 250–400k tokens, so sending all of it with every query is slow and expensive, and accuracy tends to drop when the answer is buried in the middle. Re-indexing once a month is cheap, and retrieval lets you cite the exact section behind each answer.

columns.text:
PICK: Build RAG
WHY: Retrieving relevant passages avoids repeatedly processing a 500-page handbook, reducing per-query cost and latency. Monthly updates can be indexed with version metadata, keeping answers grounded in current material with traceable citations.
columns.why: Retrieving relevant passages avoids repeatedly processing a 500-page handbook, reducing per-query cost and latency. Monthly updates can be indexed with version metadata, keeping answers grounded in current material with traceable citations.

columns.text:
PICK: Long context
WHY: A 500-page handbook easily fits into modern context windows (~250k tokens), and with prompt caching, you eliminate the engineering overhead of building and maintaining a RAG pipeline. Updating the system monthly is as simple as swapping the source document in the cached prompt rather than re-chunking and re-indexing a vector database.
columns.why: A 500-page handbook easily fits into modern context windows (~250k tokens), and with prompt caching, you eliminate the engineering overhead of building and maintaining a RAG pipeline. Updating the system monthly is as simple as swapping the source document in the cached prompt rather than re-chunking and re-indexing a vector database.

columns.text:
PICK: Build RAG
WHY: Handling a 500-page document that changes monthly would be more feasible and efficient with a Retrieval-Augmented Generator (RAG) that can dynamically retrieve and incorporate the most recent information, rather than relying on a long context window that may struggle with such a large and frequently updated document.
columns.why: Handling a 500-page document that changes monthly would be more feasible and efficient with a Retrieval-Augmented Generator (RAG) that can dynamically retrieve and incorporate the most recent information, rather than relying on a long context window that may struggle with such a large and frequently updated document.

columns.text:
PICK: Build RAG
WHY: The handbook changes monthly, making RAG more efficient for frequent updates and reducing costs compared to repeatedly processing a large context. RAG also provides better accuracy by retrieving only relevant sections.
columns.why: The handbook changes monthly, making RAG more efficient for frequent updates and reducing costs compared to repeatedly processing a large context. RAG also provides better accuracy by retrieving only relevant sections.

results.verdict: Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra both served the user best by advocating for a RAG approach, emphasizing efficiency and accuracy in handling a frequently updated large document. In contrast, Gemini 4 suggested using a long context window, which overlooks the potential challenges of processing and updating such a large document effectively.

results.question: You are doubling your price because you underpriced at launch. Do you grandfather every existing customer forever, or migrate them to the new price after 12 months?

columns.text:
PICK: Migrate after 12 months
WHY: Grandfathering forever at half price locks in a growing base of unprofitable customers and caps your ability to fund the product they rely on. A 12-month runway with clear notice is generous enough to preserve trust while fixing the underlying pricing mistake.

results.verdict: All three models provided the same answer, advocating for migrating customers after 12 months, and they each articulated the reasoning behind this choice effectively. A meaningful difference is that while Claude Opus emphasizes the need to fund the product, GPT-6 Astra focuses on budgeting for customers, and Gemini 4 highlights the impact on unit economics, showcasing varied perspectives on the implications of pricing strategies.
